shab-zina.title: The young man who asked permission to commit zina: persuading with mercy, not rebuke
shab-zina.eventDescription: A young man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, give me permission to commit fornication. The people turned on him and rebuked him, but the Prophet ﷺ said: “Come close.” He came close and sat down. He asked: “Would you like it for your mother?” He said: No, by Allah, may Allah make me your ransom. He said: “Nor do people like it for their mothers.” Then he asked him about his daughter, sister and aunts. Then he placed his hand on him and said: “O Allah, forgive his sin, purify his heart and guard his chastity.” After that the young man never turned towards anything of the sort.
shab-zina.historicalContext: In Madinah; the hadith is narrated by Imam Ahmad with an authentic chain.
prophetTraits: Praying for the one who errs
shab-zina.problemType: A young person or teenager openly admits a forbidden desire or asks a shocking question, and those around rebuke them
shab-zina.responseType: Physical and emotional closeness, then dialogue through questions that engage mind and feelings, then supplication
principles: A young person's openness is a blessing that should not be met with rebuke, so the door of dialogue is not closed
Persuading through questions that let the other person reach the judgement themselves has a deeper effect
Physical closeness (“come close”, placing a hand) builds safety
Praying for the one who errs, to his face, touches the heart
modernApplications: If your son or daughter confides feelings or desires that frighten you, first thank them for their honesty before any judgement
Use questions that stir their conscience instead of handing out ready-made verdicts
If you are the one struggling with desire, imagine what you are thinking of happening to someone you love — this is what the Prophet ﷺ did with the young man
Pray for yourself with the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for the young man: “O Allah, forgive my sin, purify my heart and guard my chastity”
behaviorObservations: He stopped the rebuking and said “come close”
He spoke with him through questions whose answers he knew
He placed his hand on him and prayed for him
whatToAvoid: Shock and shouting when children open up
Giving a ruling without building conviction
shab-zina.reflection: He asked permission for the forbidden and left with a heart that no longer turned to it — because the one who answered drew close to him before preaching.

quranRefs.relevance: The ruling is clear, but the way it was conveyed to the young man was through dialogue and mercy

farah-tawba.title: “Allah rejoices more at His servant's repentance”: when you think the way back is closed
farah-tawba.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ gave his Companions an example of Allah's joy at His servant's repentance: a man in a deadly desert lost his camel carrying his food and drink. He despaired of it and lay down in the shade of a tree waiting to die — and then there it was, standing beside him. He took its reins and said out of sheer joy: “O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your lord” — misspeaking from the intensity of his joy. Allah rejoices more at His servant's repentance than this man at his camel.
farah-tawba.historicalContext: A hadith agreed upon in its core, with details in Muslim.
farah-tawba.problemType: Feeling that one's sins have become so many or so repeated that repentance is pointless, or that Allah will not accept
farah-tawba.responseType: Correcting how we picture Allah: He rejoices at your return, so return now
emotionsAddressed: Feeling like a hypocrite after repeating a sin
principles: Allah does not merely accept repentance; He rejoices at it
Repeating a sin does not close the door of repentance as long as the heart returns
Despairing of Allah's mercy is more dangerous than the sin itself
Shame before Allah should drive you towards Him, not away
modernApplications: If you returned to a sin after repenting, do not say “there's no point”; repent again immediately
Picture the man's joy at his camel whenever shame makes you delay returning
Follow repentance with a specific good deed now, for good deeds wipe out bad ones
Change what makes it easy to return to the sin (environment, app, company)
notToApplyTo: The vastness of mercy does not mean deliberate carelessness or postponing repentance
Sins involving other people's rights require returning those rights or seeking their pardon
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ chose a tangible image close to his Companions' world
He focused on joy, not mere acceptance
He mentioned the man's slip of the tongue without holding it against him, a sign of how vast mercy is
whatToAvoid: Postponing repentance until you “become worthy of it”
Treating Allah as a judge waiting for your fall
farah-tawba.reflection: You may be that lost camel — and Allah awaits your return with greater joy than its owner.

quranRefs.relevance: Addressing the transgressors as “O My servants”

qatil-mia.title: The killer of a hundred: “Who could stand between him and repentance?”
participants: The Prophet ﷺ (narrating a story from earlier nations)
qatil-mia.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ told of a man who had killed ninety-nine people. He asked for the most knowledgeable person on earth and was directed to a monk. He asked: Is there repentance for me? The monk said: No — so he killed him, making a hundred. Then he asked again and was directed to a scholar, who said: Yes, and who could stand between you and repentance? Go to such-and-such land, for there are people there who worship Allah; worship Allah with them, and do not return to your land, for it is a bad land. He died on the way, and the angels of mercy took his soul.
qatil-mia.historicalContext: A story from the Children of Israel narrated by the Prophet ﷺ; agreed upon.
qatil-mia.problemType: Someone carrying a heavy past of mistakes who feels there is no hope, or who lives in an environment pulling them towards wrong
qatil-mia.responseType: Certainty that repentance is accepted, with a decisive practical step: changing one's environment and company
principles: No sin is greater than Allah's mercy
Successful repentance needs a change of environment, not just intention
Choose carefully whom you ask: a wrong answer can deepen despair
Allah looks at the sincerity of the step, not the completion of the road
modernApplications: If you want to leave a habit or sin, identify the “bad land” in your life: people, places, apps, idle time
Look for “people who worship Allah”: company or a group that helps you
Do not listen to anyone who makes you despair of change, even if they seem religious
Start the road today, even if you are not sure you will arrive
notToApplyTo: The vastness of repentance does not cancel legal rights or the rights of the wronged in this world
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ told the story to spread hope in the heaviest cases
He showed the difference between the ignorant worshipper's answer and the scholar's
He highlighted the importance of changing one's environment as part of repentance
whatToAvoid: Making yourself or others despair of Allah's mercy
Relying on intention while staying in the same environment
qatil-mia.reflection: He died halfway, and his soul was taken among the repentant; Allah does not require you to arrive, only to walk sincerely.

quranRefs.context: After mentioning major sins including killing
quranRefs.relevance: Even the greatest sins are transformed through repentance

abubakr-umar-khilaf.title: Abu Bakr and ‘Umar's quarrel: “Will you not leave my companion to me?”
abubakr-umar-khilaf.eventDescription: Abu Bakr and ‘Umar had an argument in which Abu Bakr angered ‘Umar. ‘Umar left angry, and Abu Bakr followed him asking for his forgiveness, but he did not give it and shut his door in his face. Abu Bakr came to the Prophet ﷺ. Then ‘Umar regretted it and came, and the Prophet's ﷺ face began to change with anger, until Abu Bakr felt sorry for ‘Umar, knelt and said: O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I was the one more in the wrong (twice). The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah sent me to you and you said ‘You lie,’ while Abu Bakr said ‘He speaks the truth,’ and he supported me with himself and his wealth. Will you not leave my companion to me?”
abubakr-umar-khilaf.historicalContext: In Madinah, between the two greatest men after the prophets — proof that disagreement happens even between the righteous.
abubakr-umar-khilaf.problemType: A disagreement with a close friend, with an apology from one side not accepted, or regret after refusing an apology
abubakr-umar-khilaf.responseType: Taking the initiative to apologise, accepting apologies quickly, and remembering the long record of goodness
emotionsAddressed: Pain at an apology being refused
principles: Disagreement happens even between the best of friends; what matters is how you come out of it
Refusing someone's apology is a mistake that may itself require an apology
The long record of goodness must be present when a new disagreement arises
The admission “I was more in the wrong” dissolves a quarrel
modernApplications: If a friend apologises to you, do not shut the door; accepting an apology quickly is generosity
If you refused an apology and then regretted it, take the initiative now
In a disagreement, remember your friend's past deeds with you: is this disagreement worth erasing them?
Do not wait for proof of who was wrong; be the first to say “maybe I was the one in the wrong”
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ was angered for his companion whose apology was refused
He recalled Abu Bakr's old merit at the most awkward moment
Abu Bakr felt sorry for ‘Umar, though the anger was on his behalf
whatToAvoid: Shutting the door on someone who apologises
Forgetting a long record of kindness because of one incident
abubakr-umar-khilaf.reflection: Even Abu Bakr and ‘Umar disagreed; the question is not whether you will disagree with your friend, but whether you will leave a door open for them.

sam-alaykum.title: “Death be upon you”: answering a veiled insult without obscenity
sam-alaykum.eventDescription: A group of Jews asked permission to enter upon the Prophet ﷺ and said “As-samu ‘alaykum” (death be upon you) instead of “as-salamu ‘alaykum” (peace be upon you). ‘A'ishah said: Rather, upon you be death and the curse. The Prophet ﷺ said: “O ‘A'ishah, Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters.” She said: Didn't you hear what they said? He said: “I said: ‘And upon you.’”
sam-alaykum.historicalContext: In Madinah, amid tension with some of the Jews of Madinah.
sam-alaykum.problemType: Facing a veiled insult, hidden mockery or poisonous words in a polite form
sam-alaykum.responseType: A short reply that justly returns the offence to its owner without obscenity or escalation
principles: A reply to an offence should match it without going further
A short, calm word is stronger than a torrent of hurtful words
Gentleness does not mean naivety or ignoring the offence
Do not let someone else's offence take you out of your character
modernApplications: When you hear a sarcastic or veiled comment, settle for a short, calm reply that shows you understood, without insults
Do not answer an offence with something more obscene, even if you are in the right
On social media, your measured reply is seen by everyone and counts in your favour
If you see someone defending you aggressively, guide them gently as the Prophet ﷺ did with ‘A'ishah
notToApplyTo: In cases of harassment or real threat, report to the relevant authorities rather than only replying
behaviorObservations: He understood the offence and did not ignore it
He replied with one word: “And upon you”
He forbade obscenity even in his defence
whatToAvoid: An obscene reply or cursing
Ignoring the offence in a way that looks like weakness
sam-alaykum.reflection: One word — “and upon you” — was enough; strength lies in controlling the tongue, not letting it loose.

quranRefs.context: Manners in dealing with the ignorant
quranRefs.relevance: Turning away from the ignorant does not mean staying silent about the truth

abuhurayra-juu.title: Abu Hurayrah's hunger and the cup of milk: dignity in need
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)
abuhurayra-juu.eventDescription: Abu Hurayrah used to press his stomach to the ground from hunger and tie a stone to his belly. One day he sat on the people's path. Abu Bakr passed, then ‘Umar, and he asked each about a verse hoping they would feed him, but they did not realise. Then the Prophet ﷺ passed, smiled when he saw him, and understood what was in his face and in his heart. He took him home and found a cup of milk, and told him to call the people of the Suffah. He gave them all to drink until they were satisfied, then gave Abu Hurayrah to drink until he said: By the One who sent you with the truth, I can find no more room for it. Then the Prophet ﷺ drank what was left.
abuhurayra-juu.historicalContext: In Madinah; the people of the Suffah were poor emigrants with no family or wealth.
abuhurayra-juu.problemType: Severe financial hardship with shyness about asking, or sensing others' need without them asking
abuhurayra-juu.responseType: Restraint with a gentle hint, noticing the needy who do not ask, and putting others first
principles: Poverty does not reduce a person's dignity
The perceptive believer reads the need of those who do not ask
Blessing lies in sharing, not in keeping for oneself
The leader eats last
modernApplications: If you are in financial hardship, do not be ashamed to seek help in dignified ways, and do not despair if those closest do not notice
Train yourself to notice those around you: a colleague, neighbour or relative going through hardship in silence
When you have little, share it; there is blessing in sharing
If you are responsible for a family or team, be the last to take
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ smiled when he saw him and understood his need without words
He called all the poor, not him alone
He drank last of all
whatToAvoid: Humiliating the needy with embarrassing questions
Keeping the little you have for yourself
abuhurayra-juu.reflection: One cup of milk satisfied dozens, because the one who shared it drank last.
keywords: in need but i don't ask

quranRefs.relevance: Preferring others despite one's own need

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

umm-sulaym.title: Umm Sulaym: wise patience at the death of a child
umm-sulaym.eventDescription: A son of Abu Talhah and Umm Sulaym died while Abu Talhah was away. Umm Sulaym prepared the boy and covered him in a corner of the house. When Abu Talhah came and asked about him, she said: His soul is at rest, and I hope he has found relief. She prepared his dinner and adorned herself for him. In the morning she told him gently, giving him an example: If people lent something and then asked for it back, would they refuse? He went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him, and he prayed for blessing for them. A son, ‘Abdullah, was born to them, and he had nine children who all learned the Quran.
umm-sulaym.historicalContext: In Madinah. The account of the nine children comes from a man of the Ansar in al-Bukhari's narration.
umm-sulaym.problemType: Losing a child or loved one, with the need to break the news or support a spouse in shock
umm-sulaym.responseType: Patience, breaking painful news gradually, and using meaning (a trust returned) to soften the shock
emotionsAddressed: The devastation of losing a child
principles: Children are a trust with their parents, which their Owner takes back when He wills
Breaking painful news needs wisdom and timing
Patience in calamity is followed by compensation and blessing
Spouses support each other in loss
modernApplications: If you must break painful news, choose the time and the way, and prepare gently
Remember the meaning of a “trust” in losing children or loved ones; it turns anger into acceptance
Do not carry grief alone; support your spouse and ask for their support
Ask Allah for compensation with confidence, as He compensated Umm Sulaym
notToApplyTo: Patience does not mean holding back tears or hiding grief; the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son Ibrahim
Grief over losing a child may need specialised support, and seeking it does not contradict patience
behaviorObservations: She held together until she could create the right moment to break the news
She used an example that convinces the mind and calms the heart
She hoped for reward and did not resent
whatToAvoid: Delivering painful news all at once without preparation
Treating weeping as a lack of patience
umm-sulaym.reflection: Whoever returns a trust to its Owner contentedly is compensated by Him beyond imagining.
keywords: how to tell my husband bad news

quranRefs.relevance: A child is Allah's trust, which He takes back when He wills

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

jabir-dayn.title: Jabir's father's debt: when a son inherits the burden of debt
jabir-dayn.eventDescription: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr, Jabir's father, was martyred at Uhud with debts, and the creditors pressed Jabir hard. He went to the Prophet ﷺ, who asked them to accept the dates of his orchard and release his father, but they refused. The Prophet ﷺ told Jabir: Sort your dates into kinds. Then he came and sat on them, and measured out for them until they were paid in full — and the dates remained as they were, as if untouched.
jabir-dayn.historicalContext: After the Battle of Uhud in Madinah; Jabir was a young man supporting sisters after his father's martyrdom.
jabir-dayn.problemType: Heavy debts (inherited or accumulated) and pressure from creditors, with a feeling of helplessness
jabir-dayn.responseType: Seeking help and not evading, organising what you have, striving to repay with sincere intention, and supplication
principles: Whoever takes people's money intending to repay it, Allah will repay on his behalf
Seeking intercession and negotiating with creditors is legitimate
Organising resources (“sort your dates”) is a practical step before waiting for blessing
Blessing descends on sincere effort
modernApplications: Write all your debts in a clear list (amount, creditor, due date): “sort your dates” first
Contact your creditors honestly and ask for rescheduling or more time; do not avoid them
Ask someone with standing or financial expertise to mediate for you
Repeat the supplication “O Allah, suffice me with what You have made lawful instead of what You have forbidden, and enrich me by Your bounty above all others” while you work
notToApplyTo: For complex legal debt matters, refer to a legal and financial specialist
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ personally intervened with the creditors
He did not blame Jabir or his father for the debt
He ordered an organising step before the measuring
whatToAvoid: Avoiding or lying to creditors
Borrowing to repay debt in endless cycles without a plan
jabir-dayn.reflection: Sort your dates and measure out for people; blessing descends on whoever organises what is in their hands and is sincere in intention.
keywords: i have a lot of debt

quranRefs.context: The right of the debtor in hardship
quranRefs.relevance: Giving time is obligatory, and remitting is better

jurayj.title: Jurayj: “My mother or my prayer” — and a false accusation
jurayj.eventDescription: Jurayj was a worshipper in his hermitage. His mother called him while he was praying, and he said: O Lord, my mother or my prayer? and went on with his prayer. This happened three days in a row, and she prayed that he would not die until he had seen the faces of prostitutes. Later a prostitute accused him of fathering her child, and people tore down his hermitage. He performed ablution and prayed, then came to the baby and asked: Who is your father? Allah made it speak: The shepherd. They came to him apologising.
jurayj.historicalContext: A story from the Children of Israel narrated by the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith “None spoke in the cradle except three”.
jurayj.problemType: Conflict between personal occupations (even good ones) and the parents' right, or facing a false accusation
jurayj.responseType: Putting the mother's right before voluntary worship, and under accusation: calm, prayer, and leaving one's vindication to Allah
principles: Answering one's mother comes before voluntary worship and personal occupations
A parent's prayer is answered, so beware of angering them
Under false accusation, turn to prayer before arguing
Allah defends the truthful who are wronged
modernApplications: If your mother calls you while you are busy with work, your phone or even voluntary prayer, answer her and then go back
Do not justify neglecting your parents by being busy with “important things”
If you are falsely accused, do not lose your temper; make ablution, pray, collect your heart, then defend yourself calmly
Trust that the truth will appear, even if after a while
notToApplyTo: An obligatory act (such as an obligatory prayer whose time is running out) comes first, and the parent is answered after it or by shortening it
behaviorObservations: When accused, he did not argue but made ablution and prayed
He faced the matter calmly and confidently
He refused to have his hermitage rebuilt of gold, asking for mud as before
whatToAvoid: Putting personal occupations before your mother's call
Panic and confusion under accusation
jurayj.reflection: Jurayj's hermitage fell through a mother's prayer, and its owner was vindicated through prayer; between honouring parents and prayer, a person is protected.

quranRefs.relevance: The mother's right is great, and answering her comes before voluntary worship

ashab-ghar.title: The three men in the cave: when your hidden deeds rescue you
ashab-ghar.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ told of three men who took shelter for the night in a cave. A rock rolled down and sealed the cave. They said: Nothing will save you except calling on Allah by your good deeds. The first appealed by his kindness to his parents, never giving his family to drink before them. The second, by leaving indecency with his cousin out of fear of Allah when he was able to commit it. The third, by his honesty with the wage of a worker who left it behind: he invested it until it became camels, cattle and sheep, then gave it all back to him. The rock moved a little with each supplication until they came out.
ashab-ghar.historicalContext: A story from earlier nations; agreed upon.
ashab-ghar.problemType: A closed-in crisis with no apparent way out through ordinary means
ashab-ghar.responseType: Supplication, appealing to Allah by sincere good deeds, and doing many of them in times of ease
principles: Hidden good deeds are a store drawn on in hardship
Appealing to Allah by one's good deeds is legitimate
Kindness to parents, chastity and trustworthiness are among the greatest causes of relief
Know Allah in times of ease and He will know you in hardship
modernApplications: In a crisis, remember a sincere good deed you did and appeal to Allah by it
Start building a hidden store now: kindness to parents, secret charity, honesty no one knows of
If you employ people, the rights of your workers may be your door to relief
If you left something forbidden while able to do it, know it is savings, not loss
behaviorObservations: They turned to supplication when the means failed
They appealed by sincere deeds no one had seen
They were relieved step by step with each supplication
whatToAvoid: Despair when the means fail
Neglecting hidden deeds in times of ease
ashab-ghar.reflection: Strength did not move the rock; three hidden deeds that only Allah saw did.

quranRefs.relevance: Hidden good deeds are ways out stored up for later
